sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Cantilevered piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters are usually operated in the first mode and analysed as single degree of freedom (SDOF) systems. To improve their performance, a two degree of freedom (2DOF) system with a novel dynamic magnifier is developed by combining four bar mechanism and helical spring to act as elastic magnifier. This dynamic magnifier is attached between the base (excitation location) and the fixed end of cantilevered elastic harvester beam. To identify a suitable configuration for the dynamic magnifier, simulations are performed with two different configurations of passive mechanism, viz., 1:2 and 1:1 magnification four bar mechanisms. The natural frequencies of the first two modes obtained with 1:1 magnification four bar mechanism are close, giving good bandwidth and the mechanism is fabricated according to the simulation results. The simulated relative displacements and first two modal frequencies are in good agreement with experiments. There after macro fiber composite (MFC) with copper as substructure is used to fabricate the harvester beam within the required operating frequency range. The improvement in measured output power from 2DOF harvester over SDOF harvester is found to be $110 \%$ in the first mode and $270 \%$ in the second mode. Further, bandwidth analysis and effect of increase in magnifier mass is also investigated and performance characteristics of proposed 2DOF harvester are compared with the earlier similar harvesters. This kind of harvester with a novel four bar mechanism as a dynamic magnifier has not been reported in literature.

Keywords: vibration energy harvesting, piezoelectric composite beam, dynamic magnifier, broadband harvester, macro fiber composite

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Progress in low power digital signal processing and developments in very large scale integration system design has reduced power requirements of wireless sensors. The applications of wireless sensor networks are wide spread; for example, process monitoring, natural environmental monitoring, animal tracking and control, safety, security and surveillance, structural health monitoring, supply chain control, agricultural automation, building environment control, smart homes, identification and personalisation, warehouse inventory, etc [1, 2].

Sensors have a limited life of operation in remote applications due to the limited lifetime of batteries. Moreover, batteries are not environment friendly. Thus there is a need to replace finite power sources in portable devices by converting ambient energy into electricity through the use of an energy harvester. Vibration based energy harvesting has gained significance in the past decades. Energy associated with vibrations is dominant at resonance; hence it is intended to operate a harvester always at its resonant frequencies. Williams and Yates [3] proposed a new kind of power generator that generates electrical energy from mechanical vibrations. Roundy et al [4] studied three kinds of vibration energy harvesters, viz., electromagnetic, electrostatic and piezoelectric and stated that piezoelectric converters have more advantages because of their high power density, robustness and less complex power electronics. Further, research community in this field has started working on improving the performance of the harvester by exploring electrical and mechanical features. Renno et al [5], Qiu et al [6], Ramadass et al [7], Tang and Yang [8] have shown improvement in the efficiency of the harvester by connecting different power conditioning circuits to the output voltage from a harvester.

The conventional piezoelectric energy harvester usually consists of a cantilevered harvester beam with tip mass. Since the displacements and strains are high at the first natural frequency, these devices are usually designed to operate at this frequency and analysed as an SDOF harvester. However, the vibration available in ambient condition is mostly variable in frequency or random. Thus, a conventional SDOF harvester is ineffective in terms of output power and frequency bandwidth during these conditions [9]. To deal with this issue, a large number of researchers have studied various mechanical features of the harvester. These features can be broadly classified into configuration technique, tuning technique, dual mode technique and nonlinear technique.

Qi et al [10] designed a multi-resonant clamped-clamped harvester beam configuration, in which small cantilevers induce a wide band strain distribution in the main beam on which a piezoelectric strip is attached. Goldschmidtboeing et al [11] analysed different beam shapes and concluded that triangular shaped beams are more effective than rectangular shaped beams in terms of tolerable excitation amplitude and maximum output power. However, it was found that, the overall efficiency of the harvester is weakly influenced by the shape of harvester beam. Niri and Salamone [12] used a manually operated passive mechanism to induce axial load in the harvester beam to tune the frequency to the ambient vibration frequency. Huang et al [13] employed a stepper motor to drive a movable support, which is used to tune the harvester beam.

The concept of a dynamic vibration absorber applied to a 2DOF harvester appears to have initially been used by Cornwell et al [14]. A relationship was developed, indicating that a higher elastic modulus and moment of inertia of the secondary structure will reduce the strain in the harvester beam. It was shown that when the frequencies of primary and auxiliary structures are close enough, the output power is maximized. Rastegar et al [15] proposed two kinds of harvesters for oscillatory and transverse motion of ships. An L-shaped harvester beam is modeled and studied for its broad band behaviour by Erturk et al [16]. Ma et al [17] proposed a new structure as a dynamic magnifier called dynamic vibration absorber piezoelectric energy harvester (DVA-PEH). The structure contains four cantilever beams placed $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ apart and all tip ends meet at a common center over which a magnifier mass is placed. Achieving the required operating frequency with this mechanism appears to be a difficult task as maintaining the same boundary conditions for all cantilevers is challenging. Aladwani et al [18, 19], Arafa et al [20], Liu et al [21] achieved amplified output power with improved frequency bandwidth by attaching a dynamic magnifier to the harvester beam. Tang and Zuo [22] worked on a dual mass vibration energy harvester; this work is similar to that done by Aladwani [18], but more attention was given to optimizing the harvester for maximum power output with respect to parameters such as mass ratio and tuning ratio. Even though two useful modes were obtained, these harvesters cannot be regarded as truly broadband as the two resonances were quite far away from each other [9, 23]. Wang et al [24] stated that the damping ratio of the primary system should be less than that of the secondary system to improve output power and accordingly chose arbitrary values of damping ratio as 0.002 and 0.02 respectively. Wu et al [9] developed a 2DOF piezoelectric energy harvester with a cut-out beam. It was claimed that the first two modes were $4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ apart, this being a useful bandwidth. However, it did not show significant improvement in output voltage over SDOF harvester. Uchino et al [25] worked on energy flow analysis in piezoelectric energy harvesting cymbals and flexible piezoelectric transducers. A figure of merit was found for the output power from the harvester, which is proportional to the product of the piezoelectric voltage constant and piezoelectric charge constant. Kim and Kim [26] studied the performance of a 2DOF harvester by flipping the first two modes, i.e., in phase and out of phase modes. It was observed that in-phase and out of phase modes are almost $1 3 \mathrm { H z }$ apart.

It was observed from literature that the early works on 2DOF harvester have shown better amplification of power compared to SDOF harvester, but the natural frequencies of the first two modes are far apart and the system cannot be regarded as a broadband harvester. Even though some authors achieved two closer useful modes, significant improvement in output power is not seen. Others used complicated structures to act as dynamic magnifiers [17]. Attaining improved power output with close natural frequencies and a comparatively simple dynamic magnifier is a challenging task and is attempted in this paper.

The present work focuses on using a novel passive four bar mechanism as a dynamic magnifier to improve output power and operating bandwidth by aiming to achieve the first two natural frequencies close to each other. To identify a suitable configuration and size of the passive mechanism and harvester beam, first simulations are performed using ADAMS View and COMSOL Multiphysics 3a software packages. Using this novel passive mechanism, the first two natural frequencies can be obtained close to each other with significant improvement in output power $1 1 0 \%$ and $270 \%$ respectively in first and second modes) and bandwidth $(47 5 \% )$ . Experiments on SDOF and 2DOF harvesters are conducted thereafter to demonstrate the superior performance of this novel simple mechanism.

sections.heading: 2. Verification of passive mechanism
sections.text:
A harvester is a composite beam made of a substructure and piezoelectric material. The relative displacement between the fixed end and the free end of the harvester beam decides the performance of the harvester [18]. To verify the functioning of the novel mechanism with theory, a simple isotropic steel beam was first used to form a 2DOF system and was later confirmed by experiments. However the secondary system should have smaller elastic modulus than the primary system to produce large power from a 2DOF harvester [14]. For this purpose, in the latter half of the studies a copper beam is selected as the substructure, and MFC used as piezoelectric material to fabricate the harvester beam.

![](images/c59fd4c590e2f9536716238927279645665e8b77fb5c4baf462fd8a2f8bc1eef.jpg)  
Figure 1. Schematic of passive four bar mechanism with (a) 1:2 magnification (b) 1:1 magnification.

sections.heading: 2.1. Design
sections.text: A four bar mechanism is often used to magnify or reduce the input displacements and is referred to as pantograph in scaling applications [27]. The present work involves usage of this four bar mechanism along with a helical spring as a dynamic magnifier. Figures 1(a) and (b) shows a schematic of these passive mechanisms. The thick line represents rigid links of the mechanism and thin lines represent flexible steel beams. The dimensions of links AB, BC, CD and DA are equal and points A, B, C and D are hinged joints. In figure 1(a), the link BC is extended to point E, such that the length of CE is equal to BC. The ratio of BE/BC is two; here onwards this configuration is called 1:2 magnification four bar mechanism. The steel beam is fixed at point E and EF represents the length of the steel beam. The magnifier mass is mounted at point E and tip mass at point F. In figure 1(b), the steel beam is fixed at point C and CE represents the length of the steel beam. Here onwards this configuration is called 1:1 magnification four bar mechanism. The magnifier mass is mounted at point C and tip mass at point E. The spring is fixed between base excitation and point D in both configurations. The mechanism with spring and magnifier mass forms a primary system (dynamic magnifier) and steel beam with tip mass forms a secondary system. Both primary and secondary systems together form a 2DOF system.

sections.heading: 2.2. Simulations in ADAMS View
sections.text:
The 1:2 and 1:1 four bar mechanisms with spring and mass act as dynamic magnifier and a steel beam with a tip mass as secondary system was modelled in ADAMS View package. Initially simulations were performed for determining the approximate dimensions of 1:2 and 1:1 four bar mechanisms and their natural frequencies with a steel beam. Thereby iteratively the dimensions of the mechanisms were finalised for the operating frequency range. The dimensions of the preferred mechanism and beam are discussed in the next section for experimental verification. Simulations are performed to find the right configurations which give the essential first two natural frequencies close to each other and high displacements.

![](images/1edf9abd338d2c827c27116f9fc278d70618fb3b1967756a9acf18ae85da8773.jpg)  
Figure 2. Typical isometric ADAMS View model of 1:1 four bar mechanism with steel beam.

Figure 2 shows the typical isometric view of 1:1 four bar mechanism dynamic magnifier with steel beam model in ADAMS View. This clearly shows the rigid links, position of magnifier mass, spring (primary system) and flexible meshed steel beam with rigid tip mass (secondary system) and relevant hinge, translatory motion and fixed joints.

Steady state simulations are performed with harmonic base displacement excitation of $0 . 1 \mathrm { m m }$ and sweeping frequency from $1 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ to $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Simulations are conducted on both configurations with identical magnifier mass, spring stiffness and secondary system with same input conditions. The first two natural frequencies and model displacements are found for three different tip masses viz., 0.58, 1.16 and $1 . 7 4 \mathrm { g m }$ . In 1:2 four bar mechanism, the displacements are measured at points E (at beam fixed end) and F (at beam tip), whereas in 1:1 four bar mechanism, the displacements are measured at points C (at beam fixed end) and E (at beam tip).

![](images/2d4a3b49c35550e3ab4d9ede2f35360ed44849d48e272c5bf1440ca4e4c5aa2b.jpg)  
Figure 3. 1:2 four bar mechanism displacement (a) at beam fixed end (point E) (b) at beam tip (point F) using simulation.

![](images/29edeea60e4733c8e06115c496a6ece9fc033c3f61e0d41b81b12ce9d67c22b0.jpg)  
Figure 4. 1:1 four bar mechanism simulated displacement (a) over spring/beam fixed end (point C) (b) at beam tip (point E) using simulation.

Figures 3(a) and (b) shows the displacement plots of the 1:2 four bar mechanism at beam fixed end and at beam tip respectively for different tip masses. As tip mass is increased, the peak displacement shifts to a lower frequency and displacements at the fixed end (point E) decrease in the first mode (6.7 to $6 . 2 \mathrm { m m } \dot { } ,$ ) and increase in the second mode (1.5 to $2 . 1 \mathrm { m m }$ ). On the other hand the displacement at the beam tip increases ( $2 5 . 5 1 \mathrm { m m }$ to $2 6 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ ) in the first mode it is around $1 2 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ in the second mode as tip mass is increased. Similar trends are seen in displacement versus frequency plots at the fixed end and at the beam tip of 1:1 four bar mechanism and are shown in figures 4(a) and (b).

The input from 1:2 and 1:1 four bar mechanisms to the beam are amplified displacement inputs at fixed end of the beam. Figures 3(a) and 4(a) show displacement plots of 1:2 and 1:1 four bar mechanisms respectively at the fixed end of the beam. It can be noted that, for a tip mass of $0 . 5 8 { \mathrm { g m } }$ , the base excitation amplitude $( 0 . 1 \mathrm { m m } )$ is scaled by a factor of 67 $( 6 . 7 \mathrm { m m } )$ and 15.6 $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { m m } )$ in the first and second modes respectively at the fixed end (at point E) of the beam in 1:2 four bar mechanism. On the other hand in 1:1 four bar mechanism, for the same conditions it is scaled by a factor of 41 $( 4 . 1 \mathrm { m m } )$ and 15 $\cdot 1 . 5 \mathrm { m m } )$ in the first and second modes respectively at the fixed end (at point C) of the beam. The purpose of designing a multimode broadband harvester is to achieve close natural frequencies with significant amplitudes [9]. It is noticed that 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration gives sufficiently close first two natural frequencies $7 \mathrm { H z }$ apart) when compared to 1:2 four bar mechanism configuration where the resonant frequencies are $1 2 \mathrm { H z }$ apart. Hence, it is decided to use a 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration as the dynamic magnifier because of better broadband behaviour.

sections.heading: 2.3. Experimental verification of 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration
sections.text:
Based on the above simulations, the dimensions of the 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration are found and fabrication drawings are prepared and are shown in figure 5(a). The links are fabricated using stiff SS304 material. The helical compression spring is designed and fabricated such that the 1:1 four bar mechanism with beam operates in the frequency range in accordance with simulations. Figure 5(b) shows a photograph of the fabricated 1:1 four bar mechanism mounted on a mechanical shaker table of the cam follower type. The measured mass on the spring is found to be $1 9 0 \mathrm { g m }$ and stiffness of the spring as $5 4 9 5 \mathrm { N m } ^ { - 1 }$ .

![](images/1a8c14f9b96f6482d99ba7dc074aa25dde4e6c48d7f9ad42cd60c6434f63b9d6.jpg)  
Figure 5. 1:1 Four bar mechanism (a) Fabrication drawing (b) Fabricated 1:1 four bar mechanism mounted on shaker table.

![](images/4629eb8821d6e758c3d1f3e93087b0c724f3dedd9db52cc8298e178a119449d0.jpg)  
Figure 6. Measured displacement in 1:1 four bar mechanism (a) over spring/beam fixed end (point C) (b) at beam tip (point E).

To measure the transverse amplitude of vibrations of the 1:1 four bar mechanism, a Dytran make 3053 triaxial accelerometer of mass $6 . 2 \mathrm { g m }$ is used. From free vibration test the measured natural frequency and damping ratio of fabricated 1:1 four bar mechanism are $2 6 . 7 5 \mathrm { H z }$ and 0.026 respectively.

sections.heading: 2.4. Experimental verification of 1:1 four bar mechanism with steel beam
sections.text:
The steel beam is fabricated based on the simulations and size of that is $1 2 2 \times 2 5 . 4 \times 0 . 6 \mathrm { m m }$ . Figures 6(a) and (b) show the plots of the experimentally measured displacement at the fixed end and at the tip of the steel beam for different tip masses. Table 1 depicts percentage deviation between simulated and experimentally measured results. The trends in simulated and experimental plots are in good agreement as seen from figures (4) and (6). For a tip mass of $0 . 5 8 { \mathrm { g m } }$ , simulated and experimentally measured frequencies are $2 5 . 1 9 \mathrm { H z }$ and $2 4 . 6 6 \mathrm { H z }$ respectively for the first mode and in the second mode they are $3 2 . 2 6 \mathrm { H z }$ and $3 2 . 2 3 \mathrm { H z }$ . With increase in tip mass, the natural frequencies in the first and second mode reduce. The deviation between simulated and experimentally measured frequencies is less than $2 \%$ , both in the first and second modes. By increasing the tip mass, amplitude of the first mode decreases and that of the second mode increases. The difference in displacements at the fixed end and tip end of beam gives relative displacement. The deviation between simulated and experimentally measured relative displacements is around $2 5 \%$ in the first mode and $30 \%$ in the second mode. The deviations are perhaps due to modelling assumptions as well as machining and tolerance factors in the experimental model. The deviations reported are of the same order as in previous literature [9], where similar experiments were carried out. With increasing tip mass, the frequency gap between first and second mode decreases. The measured frequency gap between first two natural frequencies of 1:1 four bar mechanism with steel beam are in good agreement with simulations. The above study confirms that 1:1 four bar mechanism along with harvester beam can be used as 2DOF piezoelectric vibration energy harvester.

![](images/2112d5d823c48ddd3ec73fedf75f3adb4a0c4efa36ae23d4f8f3b19a1098c52b.jpg)  
Figure 7. Harvester beam simulation in COMSOL Multiphysics 3a.

![](images/d335a88641f146bf868e04ab603770015ac9129ee3818d8206ec91042666cfc1.jpg)  
Figure 8. Fabricated harvester beam with tip mass.

sections.heading: 3. Studies using harvester beam
sections.text: Initially a steel beam was used to identify the suitable configuration of mechanism to act as dynamic magnifier and also to verify the concept. But a lower elastic modulus for secondary systems (harvester beam) will give higher amplitude output [14]. For this purpose, the harvester beam is now fabricated using copper as the substructure material and MFC as piezoelectric material.

sections.heading: 3.1. Simulations in COMSOL multiphysics 3a
sections.text:
To estimate the approximate dimensions of the harvester substructure beam, eigenfrequency analysis is performed using COMSOL Multiphysics 3a finite element analysis software with the following specifications of the beam.

Dimensions of MFC: Active dimensions: $2 8 \times 1 4 \times$ $0 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ , overall dimensions: $3 7 \times 1 8 \times 0 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ . The simulations were carried out by bonding the MFC with the active dimensions mentioned to the copper substructure and with a tip mass of $0 . 5 8 { \mathrm { g m } }$ . Figure 7 shows the model of the harvester beam in COMSOL Multiphysics 3a software. The dimension of copper substructure of $1 0 9 . 5 \times 1 7 . 5 \times 0 . 5 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ gives the first mode frequency as $2 4 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ .

sections.heading: 3.2. Experimental studies of harvester beam
sections.text: Figure 8 shows the fabricated copper harvester beam with tip mass mounted on it. An MFC strip from $\mathbf { M } / \mathbf { s }$ Smart Material GmbH, Type M2814P2 piezoelectric material is pasted over it using commercial glue $^ { 3 \mathbf { M } }$ Scotch Weld epoxy DP 460. Free vibration test is performed to estimate the natural frequency of the first mode of the harvester beam with a tip mass of $0 . 5 8 { \mathrm { g m } }$ , and is measured as $2 7 . 9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . There is a difference of $3 . 6 4 \mathrm { H z }$ between simulated and measured first mode natural frequency. The measured natural frequency is higher than the simulated. This is expected as the simulations are performed for active dimensions of the MFC, whereas in experiment, MFC is bonded to the substructure with the given overall dimensions. This in turn could have increased the stiffness of the harvester beam and the natural frequency as well. This harvester beam with a tip mass of $0 . 5 8 { \mathrm { g m } }$ and first natural frequency of $2 7 . 9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ is used for experimental studies.

sections.heading: 3.3. Instrumentation and interface
sections.text:
For the given harmonic base excitation, the output voltage from the harvester beam is harmonic i.e., alternating current (AC). To obtain the direct current (DC) a bridge rectifier circuit is connected across the output voltage from the harvester beam. Figure 9 shows the complete interface of the 2DOF harvester beam with measuring instruments and Dewesoft make data acquisition system. The Dytran make 3145AG miniature accelerometer with a mass of $2 . 3 \mathrm { g m }$ was mounted on the fixture provided in the 1:1 four bar mechanism to measure the amplitude which is input to the harvester beam. The Wenglor make CP24MHT80 reflex distance sensor is placed over the harvester beam at distance of $1 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ from the tip to measure tip displacement. Figure 10 shows the complete experimental setup established in laboratory. During steady state forced vibration experimentation, the frequency is swept manually from $1 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ to $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ in forward sweep and $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ in reverse sweep with a harmonic base excitation of amplitude $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . Commercial Dewesoft software is used to read the data from the data acquisition system. Figure 11 shows plot of output voltage readings in the time domain and indicates the procedure followed to obtain experimental results. sections.heading: 3.4. Experimental study of SDOF harvester
sections.text:
The harvester beam shown in figure 8 is mounted on a shaker table with cantilever fixtures (without dynamic magnifier mechanism). The performance of SDOF harvester is studied for open circuit voltage and power by varying the electrical resistance from $1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Figure 12(a) show plot of open circuit voltage versus frequency. The maximum value of open circuit voltage at resonant frequency of $2 7 . 9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ is measured as $2 4 \mathrm { V }$ . Figure 12(b) show plot of power versus electrical resistance. The measured maximum value of power is $0 . 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at a resistance of $2 3 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The optimal resistance is given by the equation $R = 1 / ( \omega C _ { p } )$ [28, 29], where $R$ is the optimum electrical resistance in $\Omega$ , $\omega$ is the operating frequency in rad/s and $C _ { p }$ is the electrical capacitance of MFC $( 2 8 ~ \mathrm { n F } )$ . The optimum resistance is found to be $2 0 4 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . This difference between measured and calculated resistance values is observed in literature [30].

![](images/e7f2ecba631abd95a6e80bfb84211752c0c504f2a31985e72b38e38d34e685dc.jpg)  
Figure 11. Typical output voltage reading.

![](images/0452c0eccf5c30d29247f78641fbb20d7184d26501868aa352df2cb88acd2d50.jpg)  
Figure 12. SDOF harvester: measured (a) open circuit voltage (b) output power.

sections.heading: 3.5. Experimental study of 2DOF harvester
sections.text:
3.5.1. Effect of base excitation. The same harvester beam is attached on fixtures to the 1:1 four bar mechanism to give a 2DOF harvester. The performance of this 2DOF harvester is studied for different base excitations. Figure 13(a) shows the open circuit voltage versus frequency for different base excitations viz. 0.03 and $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . With increase in base excitation, the output voltage increases over the entire range of operating frequency. For a base excitation of $0 . 0 3 \mathrm { m m }$ , the output voltage at first mode, anti-resonance and second mode are $3 2 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ , $1 0 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ and $3 4 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ and that with $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ are $3 4 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ , 14 V and $4 1 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ . The increase in base excitation increases the output power from the harvester [23]. Further discussions on the performance of proposed harvester are based on the base excitation of $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . The output voltage from 2DOF harvester increases by $45 \%$ in first mode and by $72 \%$ in second mode when compared to SDOF harvester for the same given identical input conditions.

Figures 13(b) and (c) shows plots of displacement versus frequency at the tip and at the fixed end of the cantilever for 2DOF harvester. It is observed that, at anti-resonance frequency, the displacement of primary system is almost negligible. This follows the working principle of dynamic vibration absorber [31]. Figures 13(d) and (e) shows the closed circuit voltage at first and second modes respectively. With increase in resistance, the closed circuit voltage increases. Figures 13(f) and (g) shows the output power at first and second modes respectively. In the first mode the maximum output power is $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at a resistance of $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 . 1 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at resistance of $2 5 2 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . At a selected resistance of $2 1 0 { \mathrm { ~ k } } \Omega$ , the measured power versus frequency plot is as shown in figure 13(h). When compared to SDOF harvester, the output power from 2DOF harvester is improved by $110 \%$ in the first mode and by $2 7 0 \%$ in the second mode. Apart from peaks, the measured power at anti-resonance is found to $0 . 0 7 6 \mathrm { m W }$ .

![](images/6201dc4cc55d1806f225f3ccbc6892b71cd62e82e01343f84cbdb662cc7fdaf7.jpg)  
Figure 13. 2DOF harvester measured: (a) open circuit voltage for different base excitation (b) displacement at tip (c) displacement at fixed end (d) closed circuit voltage in Mode-1and (e) closed circuit voltage in Mode-2 (f) power in Mode-1 (g) power in Mode-2 (h) power versus frequency at $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

![](images/99f223b4475bdc27ade91cba1c62082aa2c6617ee25940360f53aa0fe986374e.jpg)  
Figure 14. Bandwidth at $1 4 \mathrm { V }$ (a) SDOF harvester (b) 2DOF harvester.

![](images/ed28ae7092658a499f51de2a3f8ac7955c9ccca2f121f335c99ea126e939fba0.jpg)  
Figure 15. Open circuit voltage for 2DOF harvester with different magnifier masses.

3.5.2. Bandwidth analysis. Figures 14(a) and (b) shows the open circuit voltage versus frequency for SDOF and 2DOF harvesters. The minimum guaranteed open circuit voltage from 2DOF harvester is found to be $1 4 \mathrm { V }$ at minimum point as shown in figure 14(b). Bandwidth analysis is carried out at $1 4 \mathrm { V }$ output for both SDOF and 2DOF harvesters. The bandwidth of SDOF harvester is measured as $1 . 2 \mathrm { H z }$ and that of the 2DOF harvester is measured as $6 . 9 \mathrm { H z }$ . The bandwidth has increased by $47 5 \%$ in 2DOF harvester over SDOF harvester. Even with small changes in ambient vibration frequencies, the proposed 2DOF harvester out performs the SDOF harvester in terms of both power and bandwidth.

3.5.3. Effect of magnifier mass. Figure 15(a) shows plots of output voltage versus frequency for different magnifier masses, viz., 192.3, 196.4 and $1 9 8 . 6 2 \mathrm { g m }$ . Figure 15(b) shows the enlarged view near the peak output voltage. With increase in magnifier mass, the natural frequencies in the first and second modes shift to lower frequencies. The output voltage increases over the entire frequency range with increase in magnifier mass. For $1 9 2 . 3 \mathrm { g m }$ magnifier mass, the first and second mode output voltage values are $3 4 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ and $4 1 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ and those for $1 9 6 . 4 \mathrm { g m }$ and $1 9 8 . 6 2 \mathrm { g m }$ magnifier masses are $3 9 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ and $4 2 . 7 \mathrm { V }$ and $4 2 \mathrm { V }$ and $4 3 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ respectively. This shows that the higher the magnifier mass, higher will be the output voltage from the 2DOF harvester and this agrees with [18].

3.5.4. Comparison with earlier similar 2DOF harvesters. The performance characteristics of proposed 2DOF harvester are compared with the earlier similar harvesters reported in literature and are presented in table 2. The table shows base excitation, resonance and anti-resonance frequencies, normalised power and normalised power density of different 2DOF harvesters. The power density of harvester is calculated by considering the volume of piezoelectric material. L-shaped [16], DVA-PEH [17] and Dynamic magnifier [20] cannot be regarded as broad band harvesters as the first two resonance frequencies significantly separated [9]. The cut-out beam 2DOF harvester [9] has shown closer first two resonance frequencies but has a deep valley in between them [23], where the output power is negligible. Even though the proposed harvester has shown anti-resonance at $2 8 . 8 \mathrm { H z }$ , it has produced appreciable closed circuit voltage of $4 \mathrm { V }$ at $2 1 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ leading to normalised power density of $2 3 . 2 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 3 }$ . The proposed harvester has shown superior performance over the existing 2DOF harvesters.

Overall, these studies suggests that the 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration can be successfully used as a dynamic magnifier along with the harvester beam to give higher power and bandwidth when compared to SDOF harvester. The proposed 2DOF harvester has not only shown close natural frequencies leading to better operating bandwidth, but also significant improvement in output power with a simple mechanism as a dynamic magnifier, in comparison with earlier developed 2DOF harvesters [9, 16, 17, 20]. The proposed 2DOF harvester performs effectively between frequencies of $2 4 \mathrm { H z }$ and $3 2 \mathrm { H z }$ . These ranges of frequencies are usually found in bridge vibrations [32]. Hence the proposed 2DOF harvester can be used to operate sensors which are used to monitor the health of bridges.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
A novel passive mechanism is proposed for use as a dynamic magnifier in 2DOF harvester. Simulations in ADAMS View has shown that 1:1 four bar mechanism configuration produced closer natural frequencies of first two modes than 1:2 four bar mechanism configuration. SDOF harvester produced maximum power of $0 . 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 3 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . 2DOF harvester produced maximum power of $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in the first mode and $1 . 1 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 5 2 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in the second mode. The 2DOF harvester achieved $110 \%$ improvement in output power in the first mode and $2 7 0 \%$ improvement in the second mode over the conventional SDOF harvester. Frequency bandwidth analysis at $1 4 \mathrm { V }$ (minimum guaranteed output voltage of 2DOF harvester) showed that the operating bandwidth increased by $47 5 \%$ in 2DOF harvester as compared to SDOF harvester. Further, it was also observed that increase in magnifier mass increased the output voltage over the range of frequencies considered and the proposed 2DOF harvester shown superior performance over existing similar harvesters in terms of operating bandwidth and normalised power density.
